source.title: Densing law of LLMs
source.authors: Chao-Jun Xiao; Jie Cai; Weilin Zhao; Bi-Yuan Lin; Guo-Yang Zeng; Jie Zhou; Zhi Zheng; Xu Han; Zhi-Yuan Liu; Mao-Song Sun

record.file_problem: none; the full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: The study fits conditional task loss against model scale and tests whether task performance can be predicted from that loss, using a different measure and procedure from the original pretraining-loss scaling studies.
record.gate_note: The study reports conditional answer loss scaling results and downstream-performance prediction results. It also reports capability-density trends and compression comparisons, but these do not measure the claim versions here. The density results are the paper's own findings, not results from the cited scaling-law papers.
record.test_reason: The paper mainly uses a two-step scaling fit as a tool for its capability-density metric. It does check one part of that fit: a sigmoid fitted from task loss to benchmark score on models under 4B predicts two held-out tens-of-billions MiniCPM-3 models (Fig. 2b). That check bears weakly on V6. Its loss fits use conditional answer loss on benchmark items, not held-out pretraining loss, so they do not test V1.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase omits the main conclusion. The authors' headline is the 'Densing Law': the maximum capability density of open base LLMs grows exponentially, doubling roughly every 3.3 months (about 95 days, R²≈0.91). From this they derive corollaries: inference prices fall exponentially; density growth accelerated by 50% after ChatGPT; pruning and distillation usually lower density; and training should become density-optimal. The two-step loss→performance fit is presented as a measurement tool, and they note results depend on benchmarks and reference models.
record.recipe_differences: Uses conditional answer loss on downstream tasks and a two-step loss-to-performance fit, rather than the original studies' held-out language-modeling loss measurement and compute-optimal allocation analysis.
record.method_sensitivity: The authors state that capability-density estimates and growth rates can vary with the selected benchmarks and reference models.

fits_no_version.finding: For 5M–0.8B models trained on 10–60 tokens per parameter, conditional answer loss on benchmark items is reported to follow L = aN^-α + bD^-β.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Conditional loss on downstream-task answers scales as a power law in parameters and tokens.

fits_no_version.finding: Under one reference scaling curve, open base LLMs show 'effective parameter size' ratios ranging from below 0.1 (Llama-1) to about 3 (Gemma-2-9B, MiniCPM-3-4B). The maximum ratio grows exponentially over time (A≈0.0073 per day, R²=0.912).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Capability at fixed parameter count rises over time with data and recipe improvements (Densing Law).

record.problems: The authors note that benchmark coverage is limited and possible test-set contamination can bias estimates. The larger-model prediction evidence is shown in plots, with no numeric prediction errors or uncertainty estimates stated in the text; the individual larger models are not named there.
record.rows_left_out: Capability-density trends, pricing comparisons, and compressed-model density comparisons are outside the listed claim versions and are not included as rows.

untested.parts: Held-out pretraining loss is not measured; only conditional task loss on small models (5M–0.8B).
Loss of larger runs is not predicted from the small-run power law; held-out models' losses are measured directly.
No architecture-shape comparison at fixed parameter count.
Text-only base LLMs; multimodal work is left to the future.
End-to-end prediction of downstream scores from scale (f2(f1(N))) is not validated on held-out models. No other model families are tested, and no quantitative prediction error is given.
No comparison of exponents or fitting choices. The text only remarks that benchmarks and reference models affect density estimates.

record.verdict_notes: This is borderline between T2 and T4. The scaling fit is mainly a tool, and its only validation is a figure-only, within-family check of the loss→score step. The V6 support is therefore weak. The loss used throughout is task conditional loss computed on GPT-4o-generated rationales, not pretraining loss.

versions.untested_parts: The study measures conditional loss on downstream test tasks, not held-out pretraining loss on a validation corpus.
It predicts downstream task performance from conditional loss for larger models; it does not report predicting the larger runs' loss from power laws fitted on small runs.
No fixed-compute parameter/token allocation sweep or compute-optimal split is tested.
No controlled comparison of depth, width, or other architecture choices at fixed parameter count.
No other modalities or training regimes are tested.

The study tests predictions of benchmark performance from conditional task loss for two larger models; it does not test downstream performance across a broad range of scales or against conventional held-out pretraining loss.

The study notes that benchmarks and reference models can affect density estimates, but does not compare fitted exponents or compute-optimal splits across fitting choices, nor test systematic curve bending.

labels.label: supports
labels.condition: MiniCPM-3 family; sigmoid loss→score fit on models under 4B; two held-out tens-of-billions models; MMLU, BBH, MATH, HumanEval, MBPP and their average
labels.reason: R7–R12 and Section 3.2 support downstream predictability from measured conditional task loss in this setting. Figure 2(b) includes all six panels; the authors report effective prediction without numerical prediction errors.

relation.reason: Although scaling fits serve the capability-density method, Section 3.2 independently checks loss-to-performance prediction on two larger models excluded from fitting.

tranche.reason: The held-out loss-to-score check addresses downstream predictability using conditional downstream task loss and sigmoid fitting, a different method and measure from the original pretraining scaling analyses.

source_check.notes: The held-out evidence validates only conditional task loss→score, with no numerical error estimates; it does not establish prediction from held-out pretraining loss or end-to-end prediction from parameter count. Section 3.2 says three tasks, but Figure 2 shows five benchmarks and their average.

statements.correction: Section 2.1 defines S=f2(f1(N)). Section 3.2 reports held-out prediction of performance from task loss using a loss–performance curve fitted on models below 4B. No held-out end-to-end parameter-count-to-loss-to-score validation is reported.
statements.problem: The paper does not explicitly list f2(f1(N)) as unvalidated. Lack of a reported held-out end-to-end check is an inference from its methods and validation description.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: Held-out larger MiniCPM-3 models across the reported downstream benchmark panels
reader_labels.reason: The authors state that performance estimates based on conditional loss effectively predicted the larger models' downstream performance; see R7–R12.
